title: Edo Egusi Soup
author: Ozoz Adeniyi
desc: Four cups of egusi worked into a thick paste and lowered into seven or eight cups of stock a teaspoonful at a time, kept whole — knots of cream through the soup.
longDesc: This is the Edo way with egusi, and it is a matter of keeping the seed in discrete pieces rather than letting it disperse. Four cups of ground melon seed are worked with a cup of blended onion and chilli into a thick paste, then spooned into the simmering stock a teaspoonful at a time and left alone for twenty to thirty minutes while the mounds cook through. Three leaves follow in order: pumpkin, waterleaf, then bitter leaf with the lid off. The author calls the result knots of cream, and it feeds six to eight.
ingredients: 4 cups egusi (melon seeds), dry-ground or milled
1 cup blended onions and fresh chilies, to taste (about 5 small onions)
Cooked meat and fish, quantity and variety to preference — beef, tripe, stockfish, oxtail, biscuit-bone, snails and pomo
steps: Make a thick paste of the ground egusi and the blended onion and chilli mixture.
Heat the palm oil on low-medium for a minute and add the une or iru.
Scoop teaspoonfuls of the egusi paste into the stock, keeping the pieces whole.
Simmer 20 to 30 minutes, until the balls cook through — they change from a thickened, orange appearance.
Gently add the cooked meat and fish, and season.
Add the pumpkin leaves, then the waterleaf. Stir, cover, and cook 5 to 10 minutes until wilted.
Finish with the bitter leaf, lid off, for another 5 to 10 minutes.
chefTips: A teaspoon, not a tablespoon. The mounds want to be small enough to cook through in twenty to thirty minutes.
Lower them in and leave them. Stirring at this stage is how you end up with the dispersed, watery style instead.
A thick paste, not a batter. If it will not hold its shape on the spoon there is too much liquid in the onion blend.
Leaves in order: pumpkin first, then waterleaf, then bitter leaf. Waterleaf releases water, which is why it follows rather than leads.
Lid off for the bitter leaf. Covered, the bitterness concentrates — the same principle as the ten-minute open par-boil in NGA038.
Une is the Edo word for iru, fermented locust bean. Two teaspoons of the fresh kind is a small amount with a large effect.
Seven to eight cups of stock to four cups of egusi is a generous ratio. The balls need room, which is the opposite of what a thick caked egusi needs.
commonMistakes: Scooping with a tablespoon, so the centres stay raw.
Stirring once the mounds are in.
A paste too loose to hold its shape.
Covering the pot for the bitter leaf.
sources: Adapted from 'Traditional Nigerian Edo Egusi Soup', published on kitchenbutterfly.com. ATTRIBUTION: the page byline prints as 'By Kitchen Butterfly' — the site name — and NOT 'Ozoz Sokoh'. Two independent research passes checked nine pages on that site and none carried her personal byline; her name appears only in the footer or bio. Credited to the site accordingly, with Sokoh noted as proprietor. The page reports Published Jan 14, 2014 and Modified June 3, 2026, that modification date being part of a site-wide bulk stamp and therefore not reliable for provenance.

Quantities as printed: 1 cup of blended onions and fresh chilies, to taste (about 5 small onions); 4 cups of egusi (melon seeds), dry-ground or milled; 1/2 – 1 cup palm oil; 2 teaspoons fresh Une (iru, locust beans); pinch of salt; ground crayfish to taste; 7 – 8 cups of stock; cooked meat and fish, 'quantity and variety to personal preference'; 2 cups Pumpkin leaves (ugu), cut; 1 cup Waterleaf, cut; 3 tablespoons Bitter leaf, washed.
YIELD — GIVEN, which is rare: the author states in her comments that it fed '6–8 people'.

Times and cues as printed: simmer 20 to 30 minutes until the balls cook through; the cue is the egusi balls changing 'from a thickened, orange appearance'; leaves 5 to 10 minutes until wilted; bitter leaf lid off another 5 to 10 minutes.

THE REGIONAL CLAIM, as printed: the Edo version forms egusi into distinct balls lowered into simmering stock, unlike the Igbo version where the egusi disperses evenly, and similar to Yoruba preparation — producing 'thickened balls' that create visible 'knots of cream'. Traditionally served with pounded yam.

ETHNOGRAPHIC DISAGREEMENT, not reconciled: this page assigns the watery, dispersed style to the IGBO. Sisi Jemimah, a Yoruba author who prefers the watery style, calls it 'very much like Egusi Ijebu' — that is, Yoruba (NGA013). Two sources assign the same technique to different peoples.
NOTE: 'Cooked Meat & fish, quantity and variety to personal preference' and 'Ground crayfish, to taste' are unquantified on the page and are reproduced as printed.

ON UNE: the author places herself in Igarra, Edo State, and gives une as the word her household uses for iru. A separate article on the same site identifies iru as the fermented seed of Parkia biglobosa, the locust bean.
storage: 4 days refrigerated. The balls firm up and hold.
reheating: Low heat, no stirring, so the mounds survive.
healthBenefits: Melon seed is high in protein, magnesium and zinc.
Three different leaves give a broad micronutrient range.
Fermented locust bean contributes B vitamins and glutamates.
culturalNote: Knots of cream is the author's phrase for what distinguishes this soup, and it captures the whole intention: the egusi is meant to be encountered in pieces, soft set mounds you break into with the swallow, rather than as a uniform thickness. That the Edo and the Yoruba do it this way while the Igbo disperse theirs is one of the cleaner regional distinctions in Nigerian cooking — though the sources disagree about who belongs on which side.
